Main feedback (1/3): Devote efforts to clarify the abstract. An important thing to carry with you is to remember that the audience is missing a lot of the context that we have, and getting a feel for what needs to be included so they can understand our idea is one of the hardest things about technical writing! Clarifying the abstract will help make the "angle" of the story clear, and that will help you contextualize everything follows! 

What is the story? Well, we want to learn a parametrically robust controller for (in the end) nonlinear systems like Cartpole (and beyond!). To do this, we want to iteratively adjust our training distribution in order to promote greater robustness in the learned policy, via the proxy of level-set-based domain randomization.

One such story: @[5f6e41173e579e0001f11b71]

0a) General setting: effective control for closed-loop / feedback systems is important across science and engineering disciplines. However, many systems are complex, nonlinear, and even potentially lack model-based representations. How do we construct effective controllers for these settings? 
0b) One popular answer is to learn from data (ML / RL / etc). However, the robustness and safety of these policy synthesis methods is often unclear, due to the randomness in the draw of data, and the minimal structural assumptions on the control logic (e.g., when the policy is a neural network). 
1) Thus, our Goal: robust / safe / stable controller learned from data / simulation
2a) Problem 1: how to validate that a controller has these properties? ["Open-loop" Evaluation]
2b) Problem 2: how to learn a policy which better displays these properties? ["Closed-loop Evaluation"]
3) Idea: use evidence derived from rigorous evaluation (the 'open-loop proxy') to guide the data collection (the closed-loop data collection process)!

See previous comments for good material for the Motivation. 

Let's then put the Problem Formulation in its own section, so that we can be very precise about what we're proposing to do!
This is really great info for a 'running example' or 'test problem' subsection

This is a really good scaffolding of the idea, and works better as a list (e.g., \begin{itemize}). Let's add some context for the reader: 
\item \textbf{Control} -- the low-level feedback loop of the robot policy operating on in the physical environment
\item \textbf{Evaluation} -- the mid-level feedback loop to estimate the performance level set of the current robot policy to guide collection of training data
\item \textbf{Improvement} -- the high-level process to close the joint policy synthesis -- evaluation feedback loop. 

This example of adding context helps with clarifying the technical notation

Technical notation is always tricky, especially when there are multiple contexts to consider. Let's move this to a separate subsection that comes after we explain the idea of the feedback loop. Then, the reader will be more easily able to map the idea to the notation. For the purposes of the proposal, this might work better as another itemize, so that it matches the low-, mid-, and high-level structure of the feedback loop idea

To clarify what I mean: we know that $k$ is the iteration number of the 'high-level' feedback loop, whereas $H$ is the horizon of the low-level policy rollout. But a reader won't know that immediately. Similarly, we know that 'condition' means both system parameters (mass, length, etc) and random ICs (like initial angle), but the reader won't!

One nice trick for material like this is to pose "Research Questions" as a means of organizing our hypotheses. These can be relatively open-ended, especially for the proposal. 

For example, I think an accurate interpretation of what the current text is proposing is something like ("RQ" means "Research Question"): 
RQ1: Using standard RL approaches for policy synthesis (e.g., PPO), can we increase  parametric robustness through targeted adaptation of the training distribution? [Empirical]

What other questions might we want to ask? (One hint: propose a question that would end with "[Theoretical]" instead of "[Empirical]"). There are many good answers here!
An idea: given the above comments about the low-, mid-, and high-level feedback loops, maybe we eventually organize the related work similarly!
One other concrete idea for the course foundation is to apply this logic to learning linear systems (as opposed to the nonlinear cartpole). What if we simplified to x_{t+1} = A(z)x_t + B(z)u_t?

This will be very closely related to Tesshu Fujinami's recent works: 

1) https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.24371
2) https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.16300

During the ideation / drafting process, having bullet-point-like sentences is fine. However, linking back to the general challenge of meeting the audience where they are, remember that bullet points that make sense to you are even less likely to make sense to the audience, because they rely even more strongly on implicit context. So, some of these sentences are unlikely to make sense to Nik, for example.

\begin{abstract}%
A frozen controller's failures across operating conditions form a map of where it
works. We propose to investigate whether training near an estimated performance
boundary expands that region while limiting regression where the controller was
already acceptable. We certify the region of a frozen policy, feed that estimate
into the choice of training conditions, and re-certify on fresh data. Monotonic
improvement is the ambitious target, not an assumption.%
\end{abstract}
